robustness_note: tau=0.72 is a sensitivity check, not a threshold search -- tau=0.70 is the reported result. The perturbation flips gemma-scope-2b L10/U603 (boundary case, sim(desc1,desc2)=0.7097 vs tau=0.70) AND gemma-scope-2b L0/U10531 (2->3 survivors) -- a genuine multi-neuron perturbation, not an isolated single-point change. Correlation moves from rho=1.00 (n=4) to rho=0.90 (n=5, p=0.037): the result is not an artifact of the borderline neuron's exact classification.
provenance: PRISM paper's own human study (Sec. 4 / Appendix A.8): 7 participants (PhD/working students, no co-authors), 8 instances, 5 clusters each. Verified against paper-cited example values (see module docstring).
human_score_scale: 11-point, 0.0-1.0 (paper's pairwise-similarity rating average); stored locally as integer 0-10, divided by 10 here. HIGH = monosemantic/coherent, LOW = polysemantic/diverse.
prism_poly_used: prism_poly = mean_similarity (plain mean pairwise cosine similarity, pre-filter) from pairwise_similarities_dataset.csv -- same direction as the human score (HIGH = monosemantic). NOT diversity_score.
interpretation: Do NOT lead with 'rho improved from 0.826 to 1.00' -- with n=4 surviving neurons the filtered correlation is close to statistically content-free (huge CI). The supportable claim: on neurons where the filtered metric is defined, it tracks human judgment at least as well as the unfiltered PRISM score, AND the framework's exclusions are principled (0 or 1 survivors), not arbitrary -- gpt2-small-sae L5/U30319 is the all-fail/uncharacterized case, the other 3 exclusions are single-survivor neurons. The flagging behavior is the result; the near-perfect correlation is a too-small-n curiosity reported without leaning on it.
